exercise.title: Find a hidden-class break in real code
exercise.instructions:
Take a browser-side normalization or list-rendering path that builds many objects. Rewrite it two ways: one stable shape with every field initialized, and one branch that conditionally adds or deletes a field. Warm both paths, profile them in Chrome DevTools, and treat timing as evidence only if repeated runs show a stable difference.

Acceptance criteria: use browser `performance.now()`; consume results so dead-code elimination cannot remove work; record at least five warmed runs; identify the property-access call site that becomes polymorphic; and state why this V8-specific optimization must not dictate architecture without a measured bottleneck.
exercise.deliverable: A printed millisecond delta between the stable and unstable versions, plus one sentence naming which call site became polymorphic and why.
hints: Keep the property-assignment order textually identical across every call site for the 'stable' version, order, not just names, defines the shape.
Run each benchmark loop at least twice in the same process; the first run pays warm-up cost from the JIT.

If you don't see a difference, the loop body may be too trivial for V8 to bother deoptimizing, try reading the property back out and using it in a way that can't be optimized away, like summing into an accumulator.

questions.prompt: What triggers a new hidden class for an object?
choices: Adding a property with a new order or name pattern
questions.correct_answer: Adding a property with a new order or name pattern
questions.explanation: The misconception: assuming hidden classes track values or types, not structure. Like the warehouse shelf plan, it's the *layout* (which properties, in which order) that defines the class, regardless of what's stored in each slot.
questions.learning_objective: hidden classes are keyed by property order/shape, not values

questions.correct_answer: A per-call-site memo of which hidden class was seen and where to load a property, speeding monomorphic access until a new shape appears.
questions.explanation: The misconception: thinking of it as a general property lookup cache. It's scoped to one call site and one shelf plan, the forklift's memorized shortcut for aisle 2, valid only while every box follows the same plan.
questions.learning_objective: inline caches are per-call-site and per-shape

choices: Properties move to the prototype always
questions.explanation: The misconception: blaming garbage collection or boxing. The real cost is the forklift re-checking the shelf plan on every trip once a call site sees more than one shape, instead of using its memorized shortcut.
questions.learning_objective: multiple shapes at one call site defeat the inline cache

questions.prompt: A hot object path repeatedly runs `delete record.debug`. What is the most likely V8-specific risk?
choices: The object may move to a slower dictionary-like property representation
The property is deleted only after garbage collection
Every number on the object becomes a BigInt
questions.correct_answer: The object may move to a slower dictionary-like property representation
questions.explanation: The misconception is viewing delete as a free inverse of assignment. In V8, repeated shape mutation can abandon fast-property layouts and invalidate optimized assumptions at access sites.
questions.learning_objective: deleting properties can force slower object representations and deoptimization

questions.prompt: A benchmark shows a 12% V8 improvement after normalizing object shapes. What evidence is still required before making the pattern a team-wide architecture rule?
questions.correct_answer: Verify the path is a real production bottleneck with profiles or field telemetry, repeat the benchmark with warm-up and result consumption, and check behavior on supported non-V8 engines. Keep the optimization local unless user-visible evidence justifies a broader convention.
questions.explanation: The misconception is promoting one engine microbenchmark into universal design guidance. Hidden classes are an implementation strategy, and architecture should follow measured user impact and the supported browser matrix.
questions.learning_objective: separate engine-specific optimization evidence from general architecture rules
